page: Amazon Web Services m8gb.24xlarge is a general-purpose Nitro-based virtual server instance utilizing the 64-bit ARM architecture. It is powered by AWS Graviton processors based on the ARMv9 Neoverse-V2 core family running at 2.8 GHz. The server provides 96 dedicated physical cores and 96 vCPUs without simultaneous multithreading, supplemented by 64 KB of L1 data cache, 2 MB of L2 cache, and 36 MB of shared L3 cache. It features 384.0 GB of memory, preserving a standard 1:4 vCPU-to-RAM ratio of 4.0 GB per core. The configuration includes no onboard GPUs, lacks local instance storage, and offers a 200 Gbps baseline network bandwidth.

Benchmark outcomes show that multi-threaded computing and high-throughput memory operations represent this instance's core strengths. While single-thread testing yields average performance—such as a Geekbench single-core score of 1888.0 and stress-ng single-core score of 1706.29—multi-core execution places firmly in the top tier. It achieves 163,542.01 on stress-ng multi-core and 26,114.0 on Geekbench multi-core. Data processing workloads show strong throughput, delivering 940.69 GB/sec on multi-threaded bzip3 decompression, 92,142.0 on Clang software compilation, and 195.16 million operations per second on Redis SET tasks. Large-block memory reads achieve 481.24 GB/sec, while write operations reach 242.02 GB/sec.

From an architectural standpoint, the 96 independent dedicated cores provide linear parallelism and high resource density without hyperthreading overhead. Cost efficiency is heavily tied to its high core count and network capacity, making it resource-effective for throughput-intensive microservices, enterprise application tiers, and distributed data processing. However, applications requiring direct NVMe ephemeral disks will need external network-attached volumes, as no local storage is bundled with the instance.

The m8gb.24xlarge is best suited for large-scale multi-threaded workloads, including Clang compilation pipelines, high-concurrency Redis caching instances, large database backend deployments, static web serving infrastructure, and CPU-based LLM token generation for medium to large models.
